This article misses a key point of view. Rent regulation is effectively a public taking of private property rights. Ask any economist. 

Considering this from the point of the landlord. They save to purchase a property and then provide housing. There is risk involved in this business endeavor. Tenants may be great and take excellent care of the property or do a ton of damage. However, with most of these rent regulations there is no effective mechanism to remove the latter type of tenant. 

Further, due to a mandated right to lease renewal the tenants effectively ’own’ the property at their legally mandated rents while the landlord continues to be responsible for the ever increasing taxes and fees set by the very entities that created rent regulations in the first place. 

Next these cities want to penalize landlords for not maintaining their housing , but never recognize there is no profit left between the low rents and rising taxes and other expenses (water, sewer, fuel, insurance, etc). Also, these same cities do not hold themselves accountable in the same manner. Just look at NYCHA in NYC where simple repairs can take years.  

Let’s keep in mind the landlord actually holds legal title to these buildings and should be able to rent them at market rates or sell when they want. Tenants should have a right to occupy at market rates for the term of their contract. If they can’t afford the rent move to a more affordable place.

Here is an important aspect of the bond market that cannot be ignored: as US treasuries of all durations expire, they have to be refinanced at higher rates because the country does not have the cash to retire the debt.  This is distinctly different from municipal bonds for a school project which has a debt service structure that includes principal and interest so the debt will eventually be retired.

There is a lot of focus on the 10-year treasury rate because it is the benchmark for lending (X over cost of funds is the equation for your 30 year mortgage), but much of US debt is shorter term (3 mo, 6 mo, 1 yr, 2 yr, etc). Auctions are held every week and the US Treasury often has to buy back bonds if the market is soft.

Basically, we as a nation are trapped in a $40 trillion interest only loan that we keep refinancing at higher and higher rates. If the US government sees further reductions in revenue from job losses or a recession, debt servicing this increasing burden will become a problem without a solution.

That $billions were squandered is, unfortunately, true. Incompetence was widespread, even among units that we might anticipate to be technically adept - one example sticks in my mind, a canal entry gate in Herat province pointing its US Army Corps of Engineers plaque skyward, having been undermined by the first Spring flood. But... Speaking with older women in Balkh province who were overjoyed to have gained literacy and numeracy because male shopkeepers no longer were able to bamboozle them. Or watching women toil under blazing skies in Herat province, hand-harvesting the 3 stamens in a crocus flower that would subsequently be exported as saffron, earning a relatively good living from their Labor. Or watching teen girls taking an exam, exercise books on laps while they sat under a tree in Badakhshan province. I'm desolated by knowing that for most of these women, their lives are lived in shadows, their hopes shattered. Yet as this report demonstrates, resistance and resilience are rooted in the population. It would be unsurprising if the (Shia) Hazara, who were consistently focused on education - and who had a female governor in Bamiyan province - have more daughters in school than the other (Sunni) tribes.

That makes Nancy Pelosi’s endorsement difficult for me to understand. I admire Pelosi’s fighting spirit, political skill and ability to get things done. But given the long-running speculation about her daughter succeeding her, it is hard not to wonder whether Wiener’s decision to run before that succession was settled played a role.

One recent, wonderful nonfiction novel was about longitude and how an accurate watch was developed to determine position within the Lat/Long system overlaid on Earth's geography and daily rotation. Its innovation led to precise engineering in many other inventions and was just as important to our era as computers are.

The conflict arises with clockwork solar system modelling, which led to scientific method modelling and a manifesto that Isaac wrote for his fellow theorists to follow. This is why many contributors are so exercised about bypassing the sunrise-noon-sunset cycle as a cause-and-effect for one rotation. 

Before accurate clocks emerged, Ptolemy's framework could predict astronomical events like lunar eclipses (one occurred this week) as calendar dates. This system used the Sun's motion to define the orbital plane for Earth's orbital motion, which could then be compared with the orbital motions of the other planets.

Clockwork solar system or RA/Dec modelling turned Earth's rotation into a clock and projected its daily rotation characteristics into space as a rotating celestial sphere. It allowed observers to predict the exact times of an astronomical event, not just the date. What it could not do was model the Earth's daily and orbital motions, and why contributors here no longer associate the experience of one 24-hour day with one rotation.

We were supposed to cruise from Bucharest to Budapest in late July. Then our boat, the Viking Ullur, ran aground in the Danube the night before we were to set sail.

Viking pivoted to the bus tour model. From Bucharest (3 nights) we spent 2 nights in Sofia, 2 nights in Belgrade, then on to Bucharest for the final 3 nights.

We missed out on special experience of river travel. The bus rides (in triple-digit temps) could feel long and tedious, despite Viking's efforts to break them up with a tour/lunch stop each day, and to half-fill the buses so people had a little room to breathe.

On the other hand, the hotels Viking selected were outstanding and smack in the middle of each city's action. Logistics, at least in our experience, were nearly seamless. Our tour guides were kind, knowledgeable and lots of fun. We shared with our fellow travelers who became great, if temporary, friends. Viking also refunded about 60% of our purchase price as a future trip credit.

It wasn't what we signed up for and it wasn't for everyone. I wouldn't want to be on that bus in my 80s. There was plenty of grousing, which was to be expected.

But on the list of travel snafus, this has to rank near the bottom. We stayed in great places, explored great cities and got to meet kind, generous people. We had a wonderful time and earned a great story to share.

"Egeszsegedre!"

AI creates a bespoke solution for problems / shapes that already exist. Need a dashboard? It won’t suggest “here’s a standard dashboard template we’ll reuse, let’s just fit it to your data where needed” it builds the entire thing from scratch. 

That’s crazy inefficient - and it isn’t going to take long for large organizations to do what they’ve always done: move from bespoke high-cost/token builds to prepackaged solutions. 

TLDR - current use of AI is like the days of hand built horseless carriages. That will give way to efficient and standardized assembly line work.

However, to place non-text content on the Internet, one should be required to provide real identification. In the age of AI and fake videos, we must be able to identify people who put criminal non-text content on the Internet.

Today, we have seen AI generated videos of politicians saying things they never said. This is real. It is happening. No one should be allowed to place such a video on the Internet without supplying their real identity so they can be held responsible.

Free political speech is important, so we must exclude text-based content from this registration requirement.

comments.name: Alex
comments.body: The Norwegian Royal history is very interesting, mostly because there isn’t much of one. This article states that it’s mostly ceremonial “nowadays,” but actually the deceased King was only the third king in the “reborn” Norwegian monarchy, and the first born back in Norway. His father was born in England, as the “first new” Norwegian queen was born Princess of Wales. Before her husband (who was a lesser son of the king of Denmark), the Norwegian monarchy hadn’t existed for I think 500+ years. They CHOSE that Prince of Denmark *because* his wife was part of the British royal family. By the time the Norwegian monarchy was reestablished (between 1900-1910), it was all part of the push for Norwegian independence, so the monarchy never really exerted any actual power—since they came back 120 years ago they have ALWAYS been ceremonial. They haven’t been “true” monarchs since 600+ years ago. Anyways, play MapTaps for fun facts like this! Fascinating!

The new king's grandfather was famous for cross-country skiing around Oslo on Sunday afternoons. Many met him on skis! (I met King Haakon's mother 35 years ago on the Norwegian / Icelandic project that sent three Viking ships from Bergen to Washington.) I treasure this book. I was afraid to read it because I can't bear books (or movies) in which animals are brutalized. I still have nightmares about reading Black Beauty as a young girl. Etna was none of that. 
There is much to di9scuss, as your suggested questions indicate, but one element impressed me about this wonderful, brave dog: his lack of complaint, his acceptance of whatever is  happening to him, his patience. Human soldiers would complain, would rage, would blame, and finally would be depressed, would fear death. Etna is motivated most all by his desire to please; to do the job he was trained for and do it to the best of his increasing diminishing abilities. He has empathy, he has love for this fellow creatures, human and animal. He does not complain.
One other thought. When Etna kills, it is not with hate, it is simply what he was taught he is supposed to do. To me that raised an interesting question. Should he have had qualms? Something to discuss perhaps..

The Plague Dogs escape from a laboratory, another form of war, and attempt to find their way home too. Adams also wrote Shardik, a bears perspective. Adams is a genius at anthropomorphizing animals and their concerns and struggles.

Everyday the news is full of reports of humans suffering, feeling through the atrocities of wars. But to spend hours reading about war from the viewpoint of a sensitive, moral dog is more pain than I could endure; it would force me to acknowledge we ordinary humans have no more power to affect wars than have dogs.

It has been a year, I think, since I last read a book. I don't know where my attention span and ability to not nod off have gone. I decided to give reading another shot after reading the Times review, bolstered by my enthusiastic love for dogs. (My wife won't touch it: "Do any dogs die?")

Etna is a short, light read. Before I knew it, I was two thirds of the way through the book, and cruising to the finish on day 2. I was in tears twice: at the end of the first chapter, and again at the end.

There is horror; there is blood; there is love; there is trust; there is distrust; there is wonder; there is empathy; there are so many emotional notes, and the ending is exquisite.

My wife may never read this book, but I'll read it twice. And to anyone who loves dogs, or just a good, easy read: heartfully recommended.

comments.body: Do you remember smoking sections on planes? I was to teach a course in IVF in post Apartheid South Africa at the end of 1994 taking my then husband and 4 year old son, I was 20 weeks pregnant. My doctor was most concerned with the 17 hour flight recommending being rested and hydrated. The flight over was fine. The pregnancy was not restricting and along with the week long course, I consulted at 2 hospitals in Johannesburg and Cape Town.we rented a car driving to Kruger National Park spending a week staying in campgrounds and seeing animals out in the wild, then drove to the Cape of Good Hope. After a send off dinner, we spent our last day, now 25 weeks pregnant touring Soweto the huge Black township with a press crew. At the airport for our midnight flight i found out we were seated one row behind the smoking section. We were all exhausted and my son had a melt down. I tried to get us moved no avail. An announcement was made, not to lie down in aisles, I  could not get comfortable, and was  nauseous from the smoke, I walked to the back of our section and leaned on the bulkhead and suddenly felt so relaxed, waking up on the floor after fainting with concerned flight attendants asking will the plane have to make an emergency landing? I explained my condition, they found me three seats together far from the smoking section and I laid down and slept.

comments.name: Max
comments.body:
I think that the English-speaking coverage of King Harald’s death has been quite insensitive and disappointing because so much of it has been framed around the apparent scandals of Jeffrey Epstein and Marius Borg Høiby, when the King had nothing to do with either of those things. 

His daughter-in-law was the one who was emailing and had a friendship with Epstein. Her son, from a previous relationship, who isn’t a royal, was convicted of various counts including rape. King Harald has nothing to do with either of these things and for the sub headline to feature Jeffrey Epstein’s name, and to include Epstein articles as “related coverage” is just misleading. It’s pulling focus from a monarch who was well respected, beloved by his people, and known for an incredibly peaceful and long reign. He united and openly wept with the people in the aftermath of the worst terror incident in the nation’s history. He was outspoken about tolerance and unity. The most controversial thing he did was marry a commoner. Reducing his 30+ year reign to “[…]an incendiary association with Jeffrey Epstein” is in such poor taste.
